question: Nico controls Analia's [Bane Alley Blackguard] enchanted with their [Corrupted Conscience]. Analia casts their own [Lay Claim], targeting Nico's Corrupted Conscience. After it resolves, who controls the Bane Alley Blackguard? Who controls the Corrupted Conscience?
answer:
Analia controls both. After Lay Claim resolves, Analia controls Corrupted Conscience, and because Corrupted Conscience reads "You control enchanted creature" — with "you" meaning Corrupted Conscience's current controller — Analia also controls Bane Alley Blackguard.

Why: Lay Claim enchants a permanent and says "You control enchanted permanent." Corrupted Conscience is a permanent (an Aura enchantment), so Lay Claim can legally enchant it, and on resolution Lay Claim enters the battlefield under Analia's control attached to Corrupted Conscience [608.3c]. That control-change effect makes Analia the controller of Corrupted Conscience. An Aura's controller is tracked separately from the controller of the thing it enchants, so Corrupted Conscience simply stays attached to Bane Alley Blackguard while changing controllers [303.4e]. Corrupted Conscience's own control-changing effect then applies for its new controller — as Lay Claim's ruling explains, an Aura's effect that refers to "you" affects the Aura's controller [Lay Claim ruling #0]. So Bane Alley Blackguard moves from Nico's control to Analia's.

Notes: Analia is the owner of Bane Alley Blackguard, but ownership is irrelevant to who controls it here [110.2]. Bane Alley Blackguard still has infect from Corrupted Conscience, and since Corrupted Conscience is now an Aura controlled by Bane Alley Blackguard's controller (Analia), Bane Alley Blackguard counts as modified [700.9]. Nico now controls neither permanent. This works the same at a two-player table or in multiplayer; nothing here depends on the number of players.

Timing note: I'm assuming Lay Claim resolved normally with Corrupted Conscience still on the battlefield and still attached to Bane Alley Blackguard. If Corrupted Conscience had left the battlefield before Lay Claim resolved, Lay Claim would be countered for having an illegal target and Nico would have kept nothing — Bane Alley Blackguard would revert to Analia's control anyway once Corrupted Conscience was gone.

answer_gold: Analia controls both permanents. Out of the two auras, Corrupted Conscience has the earlier timestamp, and would normally be applied first. However, the effects from both auras apply in the same layer, applying the Lay Claim's effect would change how the Corrupted Conscience's effect is applied, and applying the Corrupted Conscience's effect would not change how the Lay Claim's effect is applied, so the Corrupted Conscience's effect is dependent on the Lay Claim's effect. The Lay Claim's effect applies first, giving Analia control of Corrupted Conscience, and then the Corrupted Conscience's effect applies, giving Analia control of Bane Alley Blackguard.

question: Alan controls [Iroas, God of Victory] and 3 other enchantments. Their devotion to white is 2. They cast [Starfield of Nyx]. After it resolves, is Iroas, God of Victory a creature? If so, what are its power and toughness?
answer:
Yes — Iroas, God of Victory is a creature, and it's a 4/4.

Why: Alan controls five enchantments once Starfield of Nyx resolves (Iroas, God of Victory, the three other enchantments, and Starfield of Nyx itself), so Starfield of Nyx's static ability turns on: each other non-Aura enchantment Alan controls is a creature in addition to its other types and has base power and base toughness each equal to its mana value.

Both relevant effects are type-changing and apply in layer 4 (CR 613.1d):
- Iroas, God of Victory's own ability: "As long as your devotion to red and white is less than seven, Iroas isn't a creature." Devotion to red and white counts mana symbols that are red, white, or both among mana costs of permanents Alan controls (CR 700.5, 700.5a). With devotion to white at 2 and only these permanents, that total is nowhere near seven, so this effect is active and removes the creature type.
- Starfield of Nyx: adds the creature type back.

Neither depends on the other under CR 613.8a — Starfield of Nyx applies to non-Aura enchantments whether or not they're creatures, and making Iroas, God of Victory a creature doesn't change devotion — so they apply in timestamp order (CR 613.7 via 613.1). Iroas, God of Victory has been on the battlefield longer, so its own effect applies first (removing Creature), then the newer Starfield of Nyx effect applies second, adding Creature back. Iroas, God of Victory ends up a Legendary Enchantment Creature — God (CR 205.1b, 205.2b, 205.4b: it keeps Enchantment, God, and Legendary).

Power/toughness: Starfield of Nyx's base-P/T-setting part applies in layer 7b and continues to apply to the same object per CR 613.6. Iroas, God of Victory's mana value is 4 ({2}{R}{W}), so its base power and toughness become 4/4, overwriting the printed 7/4. No counters or pump effects were mentioned; any of those would apply later in layer 7c.

Player count doesn't matter here — devotion only counts permanents Alan controls, so the answer is the same in a two-player or multiplayer game.

question: Nathanael controls [Grizzly Bears] and [Muraganda Petroglyphs]. They cast and resolve [Crowd's Favor], targeting Grizzly Bears. Amia then casts [Archetype of Courage]. After it resolves, what are the power and toughness of Grizzly Bears?
answer:
Grizzly Bears ends up 5/4.

Why, layer by layer (CR 613.1, 613.1g):

Layer 6 (abilities), in timestamp order (CR 613.7):
- Crowd's Favor gave Grizzly Bears first strike (earlier timestamp).
- Archetype of Courage, controlled by Amia (Nathanael's opponent), says "Creatures your opponents control lose first strike and can't have or gain first strike." With the later timestamp, it strips first strike from Grizzly Bears and prevents it from having it.

So after layer 6, Grizzly Bears has no abilities at all. Note the +1/+0 part of Crowd's Favor still applies — an effect split across layers keeps applying its other parts even though its ability-granting part has been neutralized (CR 613.6).

Layer 7c (modify power/toughness, CR 613.4c), in timestamp order:
- Muraganda Petroglyphs ("Creatures with no abilities get +2/+2") is checked against Grizzly Bears' state as of layer 6, where it now has no abilities, so it applies: 2/2 → 4/4. This is the continuous-effect behavior in CR 611.3b and the color-change example in CR 613.5 — an object gaining or losing the relevant quality starts or stops receiving the bonus automatically.
- Crowd's Favor's +1/+0: 4/4 → 5/4.

Final: 5 power, 4 toughness, with no first strike.

Timing assumption: I'm assuming Crowd's Favor fully resolved before Archetype of Courage was cast, as stated. If instead Archetype of Courage were already on the battlefield when Crowd's Favor resolved, the result would be the same — Grizzly Bears still can't have first strike, so Muraganda Petroglyphs still applies and it's still 5/4.

Player count: nothing here depends on the number of players. Archetype of Courage affects creatures controlled by any of its controller's opponents, so at a multiplayer table it would strip first strike from every opponent's creatures, not just Nathanael's.

question: Albert controls [Life and Limb], [Blood Moon], and [Murmuring Bosk], that entered the battlefield in that order. Is Murmuring Bosk a creature?
answer:
No — Murmuring Bosk is not a creature. It's a nonbasic Mountain land only.

Why: both Life and Limb and Blood Moon are type-changing continuous effects, applied in layer 4 (CR 613.1d). Life and Limb has the earlier timestamp, but Blood Moon applies first because of a dependency: applying Blood Moon changes what Life and Limb applies to (it strips the Forest subtype), which is exactly the CR 613.8a dependency test.

So in layer 4:

question: Angelica controls a [Blood Moon], a [Life and Limb], and a [Sheltered Thicket], that entered the battlefield in that order. Is the Sheltered Thicket a creature?
answer:
No — Angelica's Sheltered Thicket is not a creature. It's just a nonbasic land with the single subtype Mountain, no abilities other than "{T}: Add {R}," and no power/toughness.

Why: Blood Moon says "Nonbasic lands are Mountains." Sheltered Thicket has no "basic" supertype, so it's a nonbasic land (CR 305.8, 205.4c) even though it printed with the basic land types Mountain and Forest. Blood Moon sets its land subtype to Mountain in layer 4; per CR 305.7, setting a land's subtype to a basic land type makes it lose its old land types and all abilities generated from its rules text (so it loses the Forest type, the "enters tapped" ability, and cycling), and it gains "{T}: Add {R}" from being a Mountain (CR 305.6). Setting the subtype doesn't add or remove card types or supertypes (CR 305.7, 205.4b), so it stays a land and nothing more.

Life and Limb only affects Forests and Saprolings. In layer 4, Blood Moon's effect is applied first — both by timestamp (Blood Moon entered first) and because Life and Limb's effect depends on Blood Moon's: Blood Moon changes what Life and Limb applies to (CR 613.8a). After Blood Moon applies, Sheltered Thicket has no Forest subtype, so Life and Limb never starts applying to it at all; CR 613.6's "keeps applying in later layers" rule only protects effects that already started applying, so no part of Life and Limb (creature type, green color, or 1/1) reaches Sheltered Thicket.

Timing note: this is order-independent here — Blood Moon's layer-4 effect wins regardless, since if Life and Limb had the earlier timestamp the dependency rule still pushes it after Blood Moon. A caveat on the timing you gave: because Blood Moon was already on the battlefield when Sheltered Thicket entered, Sheltered Thicket was a Mountain the moment it hit the battlefield and never had its "enters tapped" ability (CR 603.6b, 603.6d), so it entered untapped.

Nothing here changes with more than two players; these are all continuous effects on Angelica's own permanents.

question: Alfred controls a [Blood Moon], a [Life and Limb], and a 1/1 Green Saproling Creature token, that entered the battlefield in that order. What is the Saproling?
answer:
Alfred's Saproling token is a 1/1 green Saproling Mountain creature land — it's a creature and a land, with the creature type Saproling and the land type Mountain (no longer Forest), and it taps for {R} via the intrinsic Mountain ability.

Why: both Blood Moon and Life and Limb are type-changing effects, so both apply in layer 4 (613.1d). By timestamp alone Blood Moon (earlier) would apply first, but the dependency system overrides timestamps (613.8, 613.7). Blood Moon's effect ("Nonbasic lands are Mountains") doesn't apply to the token at all until Life and Limb makes the token a land, and applying Life and Limb changes what Blood Moon does to it — so Blood Moon is dependent on Life and Limb and Life and Limb is applied first.

Step 1 — Life and Limb: the Saproling token becomes a 1/1 green Saproling creature that is also a Forest land, keeping its other types (205.1b; Life and Limb ruling #3 confirms the card types creature and land with subtypes Saproling and Forest, each tied to its proper type). Step 2 — Blood Moon: the token is now a nonbasic land, so Blood Moon makes it a Mountain, replacing the land type Forest with Mountain. Its creature type Saproling is untouched, since Blood Moon only sets the land type.

Note that Life and Limb keeps applying to it even after Blood Moon changes its land type (613.6), and it applies anyway because the token is still a Saproling — so it stays a 1/1 green creature land. Power/toughness setting from Life and Limb is applied in layer 7 (613.1g), independent of the layer 4 type shuffle. It is also subject to summoning sickness as Life and Limb notes, so it can't attack or tap for mana unless Alfred has controlled it since his most recent turn began.

This analysis doesn't depend on the number of players; it's the same in two-player and multiplayer games.

question: Alex controls a [Life and Limb], a [Blood Moon], and a 1/1 Green Saproling Creature token, that entered the battlefield in that order. What is the Saproling?
answer:
The Saproling token is a 1/1 green Saproling Mountain — a land creature — with the ability "{T}: Add {R}", and it's subject to summoning sickness.

1. Life and Limb's effect ("All Forests and all Saprolings are 1/1 green Saproling creatures and Forest lands in addition to their other types") is a type-changing effect applied in layer 4 and a power/toughness-setting effect applied in layer 7b [613.6]. Because it says "in addition to their other types," the token keeps everything it already was and adds the card types creature and land, plus the subtypes Saproling (a creature type) and Forest (a land type) [205.1b], [Life and Limb ruling #3]. As a token, its base characteristics are only what its creating effect defined [111.3].

2. Blood Moon ("Nonbasic lands are Mountains") is also a layer 4 subtype-setting effect, and it has the later timestamp, so it applies after Life and Limb. The Saproling token is now a land, and it is not basic, so Blood Moon applies to it. Setting a land's subtype to a basic land type strips its old land types and the abilities generated from them, and grants the mana ability of the new type [305.7], [Blood Moon ruling #2]. So the Forest land type and "{T}: Add {G}" [Forest] are gone, replaced by Mountain and "{T}: Add {R}".

3. Blood Moon changes only land subtypes: it does not remove card types or supertypes [305.7], and subtypes keep their correlation to the proper type [Life and Limb ruling #3]. So the token remains a creature and keeps the creature type Saproling. Its power and toughness are still set to 1/1 by Life and Limb in layer 7b, and its color is green from that same effect (layer 5) [613.6].

4. Note the feedback loop is broken here: because the token is no longer a Forest, Life and Limb's "all Forests" clause isn't what's keeping it a creature — its Saproling creature type is, and Life and Limb still sees it as a Saproling.

This analysis doesn't depend on the number of players; it's the same at a two-player or multiplayer table.

question: Alannah controls [Ore-Rich Stalactite], [Life and Limb], [March of the Machines], and [Xenograft] naming "Saproling", that entered the battlefield in that order. What is the Ore-Rich Stalactite?
answer:
Alannah's Ore-Rich Stalactite ends up as a green 1/1 Saproling Artifact Creature — Forest Land that still has its own printed abilities.

How it gets there (all type changes happen in layer 4, per [613.1d], and each effect adds types rather than replacing them, per [205.1b]):

1. Ore-Rich Stalactite starts as a colorless noncreature Artifact.
2. March of the Machines makes each noncreature artifact an artifact creature with power and toughness equal to its mana value — so Ore-Rich Stalactite becomes an artifact creature (layer 4 type change; the P/T setting happens later in layer 7b, see [613.6]).
3. Xenograft (naming Saproling) makes each creature Alannah controls that type in addition to its other types, so Ore-Rich Stalactite is now a Saproling artifact creature ([205.1b]).
4. Life and Limb makes all Saprolings 1/1 green Saproling creatures and Forest lands in addition to their other types. Even though Life and Limb entered first, it can only apply to Ore-Rich Stalactite once Xenograft has made it a Saproling; I'm assuming the standard dependency treatment, under which Life and Limb is applied after Xenograft. (The dependency rule itself isn't in the provided context, so that ordering is an assumption; if you instead applied strict timestamp order in layer 4, Life and Limb would never see Ore-Rich Stalactite as a Saproling and it would just be a 2/2 Saproling artifact creature with no land types and no green color.)

Resulting characteristics under the dependency reading:
- Card types: Artifact, Creature, Land ([205.1b], [205.2b], [300.2]).
- Subtypes: Saproling (creature type) and Forest (land type), each correlated to its own card type ([205.3c], [205.3i], [305.5]).
- Supertypes: none — it is not "basic"; type changes never add supertypes ([205.4b], [305.7]).
- Color: green, from Life and Limb (layer 5).
- Power/toughness: 1/1. Both March of the Machines and Life and Limb are setting effects in layer 7b, and Life and Limb applies last, overwriting the mana-value-based 2/2 ([613.6]).
- Abilities: it keeps "{T}: Add {R}. Spend this mana only to cast an instant or sorcery spell." and its Craft ability, because gaining a land type in addition to its own types doesn't remove rules text ([305.7]). It also gains the intrinsic Forest ability "{T}: Add {G}" ([305.6]). Note it's a creature now, so summoning sickness applies to those {T} abilities.

This analysis doesn't depend on the number of players; it's the same at a two-player or multiplayer table, since all four permanents are Alannah's and Xenograft only looks at creatures she controls.

question: Ainsley controls [Furycalm Snarl], [Humility], [Magus of the Moon], and [Crosis's Catacombs] that entered the battlefield in that order. What are the characteristics of the Furycalm Snarl and Crosis's Catacombs?
answer:
Both Furycalm Snarl and Crosis's Catacombs are nonbasic lands with the single land subtype Mountain, and both have the intrinsic mana ability "{T}: Add {R}" from that subtype. Neither is a creature, so Humility does nothing to either land.

Why Magus of the Moon still works even though Humility is on the battlefield: continuous effects are applied in layer order (CR 613.1), not timestamp order across layers. Magus of the Moon's "Nonbasic lands are Mountains" is a type-changing effect applied in layer 4; Humility's "All creatures lose all abilities" is applied in layer 6. Layer 4 is applied first, at which point Magus of the Moon still has its ability, so the land-type change happens. Once an effect has started to apply, it keeps applying in later layers even though the ability generating it is stripped in layer 6 (CR 613.6). So Humility does not turn off Magus of the Moon's effect on lands (Humility does make Magus of the Moon itself a 1/1 with no abilities as a creature).

Both lands are nonbasic: neither has the "basic" supertype, and a land is nonbasic even if it has a basic land type (CR 205.4c). Crosis's Catacombs loses the Lair subtype, since the type-changing effect sets its land subtype to Mountain; Furycalm Snarl had no land subtype to begin with (Furycalm Snarl ruling #1) and now has Mountain. Being Mountains, each has "{T}: Add {R}" (CR 305.6, CR 107.4a). Neither is affected in color, card type (still just Land), or power/toughness — lands have none.

One gap: the provided context does not include the rule (CR 305.7) governing whether an effect that sets a land's subtypes also removes the land's other abilities. Under the rules given here I can only confirm the subtype change and the added "{T}: Add {R}"; in practice such effects also strip the lands' other abilities, so treat Furycalm Snarl's "{T}: Add {R} or {W}" and Crosis's Catacombs' "{T}: Add {U}, {B}, or {R}" and its sacrifice trigger as unreliable from this context. Both lands' enters-the-battlefield abilities already resolved before Magus of the Moon arrived, so they're moot now.

Assumed timing: Magus of the Moon entered after Humility and is on the battlefield now; if Magus of the Moon left the battlefield, the lands would immediately revert to their printed types and abilities. Nothing here depends on player count — the answer is the same in a two-player game or a multiplayer game, since Magus of the Moon affects all nonbasic lands regardless of controller.

question: Aiden controls [Volrath's Shapeshifter] and [Yixlid Jailer]. The top card of their graveyard is [Mistform Skyreaver]. Does Volrath's Shapeshifter have flying?
answer:
Yes — Volrath's Shapeshifter has flying (and is a 6/6 blue Illusion named Mistform Skyreaver with Mistform Skyreaver's "{1}: This creature becomes the creature type of your choice until end of turn" ability, plus its own granted "{2}: Discard a card").

Why Yixlid Jailer doesn't stop it:
- Yixlid Jailer says "Cards in graveyards lose all abilities." That is an ability-removing effect. Per [113.10] and [612.3], adding or removing abilities does not change the text of the affected object. So the Mistform Skyreaver card in Aiden's graveyard still has all of its printed text — it simply doesn't have functional abilities while it sits in the graveyard.
- Volrath's Shapeshifter is not an ability-granting or copy effect keyed off the graveyard card's abilities; it is a text-changing effect. [612.6] specifically calls out Volrath's Shapeshifter as the one card that gives an object the "full text" of another object, changing the text box, type line, name, mana cost, color indicator, power, and toughness. It reads the printed/copiable text, which Yixlid Jailer leaves intact.
- So Volrath's Shapeshifter takes on Mistform Skyreaver's full text, including "Flying," and that flying is on Volrath's Shapeshifter, which is on the battlefield, not in a graveyard — Yixlid Jailer only affects cards in graveyards.
- The condition is also met: Mistform Skyreaver is still a creature card in the graveyard. Card types come from the type line, not from abilities, so losing abilities doesn't make it a noncreature card (compare [Yixlid Jailer ruling #1], where a changeling card in a graveyard still has all creature types because that's a type matter). If the top card were not a creature card, Volrath's Shapeshifter would just be a 0/1 blue creature ([Volrath's Shapeshifter ruling #0]).
- Per [Volrath's Shapeshifter ruling #1], Volrath's Shapeshifter keeps its granted "{2}: Discard a card" in addition to the abilities from the text it takes on, and per [Volrath's Shapeshifter ruling #4] no "enters" abilities trigger from the change of form.

One caveat about the graveyard card itself: while Mistform Skyreaver is in the graveyard, its own abilities do nothing there (Yixlid Jailer). That's irrelevant here because flying is only doing work on the battlefield copy. Player count doesn't matter — nothing in this interaction depends on the number of opponents; Yixlid Jailer affects cards in every player's graveyard equally.

question: Nickolas controls [Dryad Arbor]. Aniya casts [Overwhelming Splendor], enchanting Nickolas. After it resolves, can Nickolas tap the Dryad Arbor for {G}?
answer:
No. Nickolas can't tap Dryad Arbor for {G} anymore, because Dryad Arbor no longer has a mana ability at all.

Why: Dryad Arbor is a Land Creature — Forest Dryad, and its mana ability is "{T}: Add {G}" (part of what being a Forest gives it). Overwhelming Splendor says "Creatures enchanted player controls lose all abilities and have base power and toughness 1/1." Dryad Arbor is a creature Nickolas controls, so in the layer system it loses all abilities (layer 6) and becomes base 1/1 (layer 7b). Running that through the layers leaves Dryad Arbor as a green 1/1 Land Creature — Forest Dryad with an empty ability list. It's still a land and still a Forest, but the ability that would have produced mana is gone, so there is nothing to activate — CR 602.5 (a player can't begin to activate an ability that's prohibited/nonexistent) and CR 605.2 only preserves the *mana ability* status of an ability that still exists; here the ability itself is removed.

Note that Overwhelming Splendor's other clause, "Enchanted player can't activate abilities that aren't mana abilities or loyalty abilities," would have let a mana ability through — mana abilities are exactly the kind of ability Overwhelming Splendor permits (CR 113.4, 605.1, 605.3a). But that permission is moot for Dryad Arbor because the first clause already stripped the ability.

Timing caveat: this assumes the ability was already on Dryad Arbor when Overwhelming Splendor became attached. Per Overwhelming Splendor ruling #5, if some effect *grants* Dryad Arbor an ability (including a mana ability) after Overwhelming Splendor is attached, Dryad Arbor keeps that new ability and could activate it, since it's a mana ability and Overwhelming Splendor doesn't stop those. Also, if Dryad Arbor ever stops being a creature, it would stop being affected by the ability-stripping clause.

Player count doesn't matter here: Overwhelming Splendor enchants a single player (Nickolas), so the answer is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table — only Nickolas's creatures are affected, and other players' Dryad Arbors tap normally.

question: Aspen controls [Watchwolf] enchanted by [Lignify], [Figure of Destiny] that's had its third ability activated, and [Swab Goblin]. They casts [Pack's Favor] targeting Swab Goblin. After that resolves, they casts [Mirrorweave] targeting Figure of Destiny. What are the characteristics of Swab Goblin and Watchwolf?
answer:
Both become copies of Figure of Destiny's printed (copiable) values, not its pumped-up activated state.

Swab Goblin: a 4/4 red-and-white creature named Figure of Destiny, Creature — Kithkin, with all three of Figure of Destiny's activated abilities. Its copiable values from Mirrorweave are the printed 1/1 Kithkin with mana cost {R/W} (hence red and white), because the type/power/toughness changes from Figure of Destiny's activated third ability are not copiable values (707.2, 707.2a). The +3/+3 from Pack's Favor is a non-copy effect that still applies in layer 7c after the copy effect in layer 1a (613.2a, 707.4), giving 4/4.

Watchwolf: a 0/4 red-and-white Creature — Treefolk named Figure of Destiny with no abilities. It copies Figure of Destiny's printed values in layer 1a, then Lignify (still attached, unaffected by the copy — 707.4) applies in later layers: layer 4 makes it a Treefolk (overwriting Kithkin), layer 6 removes all abilities (including the three copied {R/W} abilities), and layer 7b sets base power/toughness 0/4. Lignify even overwrites characteristic-defining abilities that would set P/T or creature types (Lignify ruling #5). Its color stays red-and-white, since color comes from the copied mana cost {R/W} and Lignify doesn't change color.

Figure of Destiny itself is unchanged (Mirrorweave affects each *other* creature): still an 8/8 Kithkin Spirit Warrior Avatar with flying and first strike.

Timing assumption: Pack's Favor fully resolved before Mirrorweave was cast, as stated. If instead Pack's Favor resolved after Mirrorweave, the result would be identical — the copy effect applies in layer 1 regardless of timestamp order, so Swab Goblin would still be 4/4.

Nothing here depends on player count; the answer is the same in two-player and multiplayer games, since only Aspen's own creatures are involved.

question: Allison controls [Dralnu's Crusade] and [Leopard-Spotted Jiao]. Allison then casts [Conspiracy] naming "Goblin". What are the creature types of Leopard-Spotted Jiao and does it get +1/+1?
answer:
Leopard-Spotted Jiao ends up as a black Goblin Zombie creature, 4/2 \'s Crusade's +1/+1 does apply.

Why: both Conspiracy and Dralnu's Crusade change types, so both are applied in layer 4 (CR 613.1d). Normally they'd go in timestamp order, but Dralnu's Crusade ("All Goblins are black and are Zombies in addition to their other creature types") depends on Conspiracy: applying Conspiracy changes the set of objects Dralnu's Crusade applies to, since Conspiracy makes Leopard-Spotted Jiao a Goblin (CR 613.8a). Dependent effects are applied afterward, so:

- Layer 4, Conspiracy: sets Leopard-Spotted Jiao's creature type to Goblin, replacing Beast entirely (CR 205.1a; Conspiracy ruling #4 \types).
- Layer 4, Dralnu's Crusade: Leopard-Spotted Jiao is now a Goblin, so it gains Zombie "in addition to its other creature types" (CR 205.1b) \u2192 Goblin Zombie.
- Layer 5, Dralnu's Crusade: it becomes black only, losing red (Dralnu's Crusade ruling #0).
- Layer 7c, Dralnu's Crusade: +1/+1, so 3/1 becomes 4/2.

Note Conspiracy sets the type continuously, so this isn't a one-shot \u2014 if Conspiracy leaves the battlefield, Leopard-Spotted Jiao reverts to a red 3/1 Beast and Dralnu's Crusade stops applying to it (CR 613.5).

This interaction involves only Allison's own permanents, so it plays out the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table.

question: Aya controls a [Skullbriar, the Walking Grave] with 3 +1/+1 counters on it. Nico casts [Duplicant] and has it exile Skullbriar, the Walking Grave. What are Duplicant's power and toughness after the imprint ability resolves?
answer:
Duplicant is a 4/4 Zombie Elemental Shapeshifter (assuming nothing else is modifying it).

Why: Skullbriar, the Walking Grave's last ability says "Counters remain on Skullbriar as it moves to any zone other than a player's hand or library." Skullbriar, the Walking Grave has that ability on the battlefield, so when Nico's Duplicant exiles it, the three +1/+1 counters go to exile with it [Skullbriar, the Walking Grave ruling #1]. A +1/+1 counter on a creature card in a zone other than the battlefield still adds to that object's power and toughness [122.1a], which is exactly why a Skullbriar, the Walking Grave with a counter in the command zone is 2/2 [Skullbriar, the Walking Grave ruling #2]. So the exiled Skullbriar, the Walking Grave card is 1/1 base + three counters = 4/4 in exile.

Duplicant's static ability then sets its power and toughness (in layer 7b, effects that set P/T to a specific value [613.4b]) to the exiled card's power and toughness, and gives it that card's creature types (Zombie Elemental) while remaining a Shapeshifter. That's a base-P/T change [Duplicant ruling #0], and it updates continuously if the exiled card's P/T changes [Duplicant ruling #3]. Note the exception Duplicant ruling #2 mentions — abilities that add or subtract power/toughness (like Death's Shadow's) don't apply in exile — but counters are not abilities; they are markers that modify characteristics directly [122.1a], so they do count here.

Any +1/+1 counters or pump effects on Duplicant itself would still apply on top of the 4/4 [Duplicant ruling #0]; the question states none.

This works the same at a two-player or multiplayer table; nothing here depends on the number of players. Timing note: I'm assuming the counters were on Skullbriar, the Walking Grave before it was exiled. If the counters were somehow added after it hit exile, they wouldn't be there (nothing places counters on exiled cards), and Duplicant would be 1/1.

question: Alijah controls [Badlands] and [Conversion]. Alijah then casts [Magus of the Moon]. After that resolves, what color(s) of mana can Badlands tap for?
answer:
Badlands taps only for {W} (white).

Why: both Magus of the Moon ("Nonbasic lands are Mountains") and Conversion ("All Mountains are Plains") are type-changing continuous effects applied in layer 4. Conversion has the earlier timestamp, but it depends on Magus of the Moon: applying Magus of the Moon changes what Conversion applies to (it makes the nonbasic Badlands a Mountain), so Magus of the Moon is applied first.

Step 1 — Magus of the Moon: Badlands loses its Swamp and Mountain types and becomes just a Mountain, losing its old abilities and gaining "{T}: Add {R}" [Magus of the Moon ruling #4], [305.7].
Step 2 — Conversion: Badlands is now a Mountain, so it becomes a Plains. Under 305.7 it again loses the land type it had and the abilities from it, and gains the intrinsic Plains ability "{T}: Add {W}" [305.6].

So Badlands ends up as a nonbasic land with subtype Plains only, tapping for {W}. It can no longer produce {B} or {R} — its printed dual mana abilities ([Badlands ruling #3]) are gone, since the type-setting effects strip abilities generated from its old land types [Badlands ruling #1]. Note neither effect changes its name or supertypes [Magus of the Moon ruling #1], [Conversion ruling #1], and there was never a window to tap it for red in between — this is a single continuous-effect calculation, not a sequence of events [Conversion ruling #0].

This analysis doesn't depend on player count: the effects are global and apply the same way in a two-player or multiplayer game.

question: Adriel controls [Wandering Ones] equipped with [Fleetfeather Sandals]. On Nico's turn, they enchant it with [Tightening Coils]. On Adriel's next turn, they activate Fleetfeather Sandals's equip ability, targeting Wandering Ones. After that resolves, does it have flying?
answer:
Yes — after the equip ability resolves, Wandering Ones has flying (and haste).

Why: Fleetfeather Sandals and Tightening Coils both affect abilities in layer 6, so they're ordered by timestamp (CR 613.7a). Originally Fleetfeather Sandals was attached first, so Tightening Coils' "loses flying" had the later timestamp and won. But an Equipment receives a new timestamp each time it becomes attached to an object — including when it's re-attached to the same creature (CR 613.7e). Activating Fleetfeather Sandals's equip ability targeting Wandering Ones re-attaches it, giving Fleetfeather Sandals (and thus its "Equipped creature has flying and haste" static ability) a timestamp later than Tightening Coils. In layer 6 the removal applies first, then the grant, so flying sticks. This matches Tightening Coils ruling #0: if an effect gives the enchanted creature flying after Tightening Coils became attached, the creature has flying.

Other characteristics: Tightening Coils' -6/-0 still applies in layer 7c, so Wandering Ones is a -5/1 blue Spirit with flying and haste. Toughness is still 1, so it isn't put into the graveyard as a state-based action (CR 704.1); its power being negative just means it deals no combat damage.

If instead the equip had been activated before Tightening Coils was attached, Tightening Coils would have the later timestamp and Wandering Ones would not have flying.

Player count doesn't matter here — the timestamp ordering works the same in a two-player or multiplayer game; note only Adriel, as controller of Fleetfeather Sandals, can activate its equip ability (CR 301.5d), and equip targets a creature Adriel controls.

question: Ari controls [Bludgeon Brawl] and [Soldevi Digger]. They cast [Titania's Song]. Once it resolves, what are the characteristics of Soldevi Digger?
answer:
Soldevi Digger becomes a colorless 2/2 artifact creature named Soldevi Digger, with no subtypes and no abilities. It is not an Equipment anymore, and it loses both its own "{2}: Put the top card of your graveyard on the bottom of your library" and the equip/bonus abilities Bludgeon Brawl was granting.

Why, layer by layer (CR 613.1, CR 110.3):

- Layer 4 (types/subtypes): Titania's Song says each noncreature artifact "becomes an artifact creature." Bludgeon Brawl only applies to "each noncreature, non-Equipment artifact." These are both layer-4 effects, and applying Titania's Song changes what Bludgeon Brawl applies to (Soldevi Digger stops being a noncreature artifact), so Bludgeon Brawl is dependent on Titania's Song and Titania's Song applies first despite its later timestamp (CR 613.6 governs how one ability's parts spread across layers; the dependency test decides this ordering). After Titania's Song applies, Soldevi Digger is an artifact creature, so Bludgeon Brawl no longer applies to it at all — no Equipment subtype (CR 205.1a, 205.1b: adding the creature type doesn't remove the artifact type, and no artifact subtype is added).
- Layer 6 (abilities): Since Bludgeon Brawl isn't applying, it grants nothing. Titania's Song makes Soldevi Digger lose all abilities, so its {2} activated ability is gone.
- Layer 7b (P/T setting): Titania's Song sets power and toughness each equal to its mana value. Soldevi Digger's mana cost is {2} (two generic), so its mana value is 2 — it's 2/2.
- Colors: nothing changes color, so it stays colorless.

Timing note: I'm assuming Titania's Song resolves while Bludgeon Brawl is already on the battlefield, as stated. If instead Bludgeon Brawl entered after Titania's Song was already applying, the result is the same — Bludgeon Brawl still wouldn't apply to a creature artifact. Also note Titania's Song's own text: if it later leaves the battlefield, its effect continues until end of turn, so Soldevi Digger stays a 2/2 ability-less artifact creature (and stays outside Bludgeon Brawl's reach) for the rest of that turn.

This analysis doesn't depend on player count; it's the same in two-player and multiplayer games.

question: Ariah controls [Wayward Angel] and has 7 cards in their graveyard. Nickolas casts [Turn to Frog], targeting Wayward Angel. What are Wayward Angel's characteristics after Turn to Frog resolves?
answer:
Wayward Angel ends up a 4/4 blue Frog creature with no abilities, controlled by Ariah.

Why, layer by layer (CR 613.1, 613.1g):

- Layer 4 (types): Turn to Frog makes Wayward Angel a Frog — it loses the Angel and Horror subtypes; it's still a Creature.
- Layer 5 (color): Wayward Angel's own threshold ability (earlier timestamp) makes it black — and only black, not white and black (Wayward Angel ruling #0). Then Turn to Frog's later timestamp makes it blue, overwriting that (CR 613.7). Final color: blue.
- Layer 6 (abilities): the threshold ability applies first (timestamp order), granting trample and the upkeep sacrifice trigger; then Turn to Frog removes all abilities. Wayward Angel has no abilities — no flying, vigilance, trample, upkeep trigger, or threshold ability.
- Layer 7b (setting P/T): Turn to Frog sets base power and toughness to 1/1 (CR 613.4b, 208.4a/208.4b).
- Layer 7c (modifying P/T): here's the trap. Even though the threshold ability was stripped away in layer 6, CR 613.6 says an effect that has already started to apply in one layer keeps applying in every other applicable layer, even if the ability generating it is removed during the process. The threshold effect started applying back in layer 5 (making Wayward Angel black), so its +3/+3 part still applies in layer 7c. 1/1 + 3/+3 = 4/4. This is the same principle as the Theros God note in Turn to Frog ruling #4.

Assumption on timing: Ariah has seven or more cards in the graveyard both when Turn to Frog resolves and afterward. If the graveyard drops below seven later, the threshold condition stops being met and the +3/+3 goes away, leaving Wayward Angel a 1/1 blue Frog with no abilities. Also note Turn to Frog ruling #0: any power/toughness-setting effect that starts applying after this will overwrite the 1/1, and Turn to Frog ruling #3: any ability granted after resolution sticks.

Player count doesn't matter here — nothing in this interaction depends on the number of opponents, so the answer is the same in a two-player game or a multiplayer game.

question: Ariella controls a manifested [Wayward Angel] and has 7 cards in their graveyard. Nathaniel casts [Turn to Frog], targeting Wayward Angel. After that resolves, Ariella turns Wayward Angel face up. What are Wayward Angel's characteristics afterwards?
answer:
After Ariella turns it face up, Wayward Angel is a 4/4 black Frog creature with trample and "At the beginning of your upkeep, sacrifice a creature" — assuming Ariella still has seven or more cards in their graveyard.

Why:

1. While manifested, Wayward Angel was a 2/2 face-down colorless creature with no name, no subtypes, no abilities and no mana cost (CR 701.40a, 708.2a). Turn to Frog resolving on it applied normally.
2. Turning it face up (the manifest special action, CR 701.40b, 116.2b) ends the face-down characteristic-defining effect and restores its copiable values, but CR 708.8 says effects already applied to the face-down permanent still apply to the face-up permanent. So Turn to Frog keeps applying, now on top of the real Wayward Angel card.
3. Applying CR 613.1 layers, with Turn to Frog's timestamp earlier than the threshold ability's (the threshold ability only starts existing/applying to a face-up Wayward Angel now, and in layer 5 it is applied after Turn to Frog):
   - Layer 4: Turn to Frog sets the type line to Frog creature; Angel and Horror are gone (Turn to Frog ruling #1: it keeps other card types/supertypes, loses creature types).
   - Layer 5: Turn to Frog makes it blue, then the threshold ability makes it black — black wins, and Wayward Angel ruling #0 confirms it is black, not white-and-black.
   - Layer 6: Turn to Frog removes all abilities, including the threshold ability itself. But per CR 613.6, because the threshold ability had already started applying (in layer 5), it continues to apply in every later layer even though it was just removed — so it still grants trample and the upkeep sacrifice trigger. Flying and vigilance are gone.
   - Layer 7b: Turn to Frog sets base power/toughness to 1/1 (Turn to Frog ruling #0).
   - Layer 7c: the threshold ability's +3/+3 still applies (CR 613.6), giving 4/4.
4. This all lasts until end of turn; when Turn to Frog wears off, Wayward Angel goes back to being a white (black with threshold) 4/4 Angel Horror with flying and vigilance.

Timing note: I'm assuming the order stated — Turn to Frog resolved first, then Wayward Angel was turned face up. If Ariella had instead turned it face up first and Nathaniel cast Turn to Frog afterward, Turn to Frog would have the later timestamp: it would then be a blue 1/1 Frog with no abilities, because its layer-5 blue and layer-6 ability removal would be applied after the threshold ability (which would be stripped before it could grant anything, and its +3/+3 would not apply since it never started applying in an earlier layer).

Player count doesn't matter here; nothing in this interaction depends on the number of opponents.

question: Ahmad controls [Conspiracy] (naming "Ferret"), [Kormus Bell], [Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth], and a [Vastwood Zendikon] enchanting Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth that entered the battlefield in that order. Is Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth a creature? If so, what are its creature types?
answer:
Yes — Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth is a creature, and its only creature type is Ferret. Its full type line is "Legendary Land Creature — Swamp Ferret," and it's a 6/4 green permanent.

How the layers get there (CR 613.1d, layer 4 — type-changing effects, applied in timestamp order except where dependency reorders them):

1. Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth's own ability makes each land (including itself) a Swamp in addition to its other land types [Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth ruling #0].
2. Kormus Bell says "All Swamps are 1/1 black creatures that are still lands," so Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth gains the creature card type while keeping Land and its Legendary supertype (CR 205.1b, 205.4b). Kormus Bell's effect is applied after Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth's even though its timestamp is earlier, because Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth's effect changes what Kormus Bell applies to (CR 613.9).
3. Vastwood Zendikon makes the enchanted land a 6/4 green Elemental creature that's still a land — briefly adding the creature type Elemental.
4. Conspiracy (naming Ferret) says creatures you control are the chosen type. It's a subtype-setting effect in layer 4, and it depends on the effects that make Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth a creature at all, so it's applied last. It sets the creature type to Ferret and removes all other creature types, including Elemental [Conspiracy ruling #4], and it can grant a creature type to animated lands that would otherwise have none [Conspiracy ruling #1].

Conspiracy sets only creature types, so the land type Swamp survives (subtypes are correlated to their card type — Swamp to Land, Ferret to Creature; CR 205.3c), as do the Land card type and the Legendary supertype (CR 205.4b). Because Swamp remains, Kormus Bell keeps applying — nothing here is circular in a problematic way, since layer-4 results are evaluated once through the layer order (CR 613.5).

Other characteristics: in layer 5, Kormus Bell's black is applied first, then Vastwood Zendikon's green (later timestamp) sets the color, so it's green only. In layer 7b, Kormus Bell's 1/1 is applied first, then Vastwood Zendikon's 6/4, so it's 6/4. It's both a land and a creature and can be affected by anything affecting either [Kormus Bell ruling #0], [Vastwood Zendikon ruling #5].

Nothing here depends on the number of players; the answer is the same in two-player and multiplayer games (Conspiracy and Kormus Bell care about permanents Ahmad controls / all Swamps regardless of player count).

question: Andre controls [Raugrin Triome] and [Prismatic Omen]. Nala casts [Blood Moon]. After it resolves, what land types does Raugrin Triome have?
answer:
Raugrin Triome ends up with exactly one land type: Mountain. Its only mana ability is "{T}: Add {R}."

Why: both Prismatic Omen and Blood Moon are type-changing continuous effects, so they apply in layer 4 in timestamp order. Prismatic Omen (already on the battlefield, earlier timestamp) first makes Raugrin Triome every basic land type — Plains, Island, Swamp, Mountain, Forest — in addition to its own types (Prismatic Omen ruling #0). Then Blood Moon resolves with a later timestamp and *sets* the subtype of every nonbasic land to Mountain, wiping the earlier-applied types. Neither effect depends on the other: Prismatic Omen doesn't give Raugrin Triome the "basic" supertype (Prismatic Omen ruling #1), and a land is nonbasic unless it has that supertype even if it has basic land types [205.4c, 305.8], so Blood Moon still applies to it regardless of Prismatic Omen.

Per rule 305.7, setting the subtype to a basic land type makes Raugrin Triome lose its old land types (Island, Plains) and all abilities from its rules text and old types — so it loses "This land enters tapped," Cycling {3}, and its {U}/{W} mana production — and it gains the intrinsic Mountain ability "{T}: Add {R}" [305.6, Mountain, Blood Moon ruling #2]. Its name, card type (land), and supertypes are unchanged [205.4b, Blood Moon ruling #1].

Order matters here: I'm assuming Prismatic Omen was already on the battlefield when Blood Moon resolved, as stated. If instead Blood Moon were already out and Prismatic Omen entered afterward, Prismatic Omen's later timestamp would add all five basic land types on top of Mountain, and Raugrin Triome would tap for any of {W}{U}{B}{R}{G}.

This analysis doesn't change with player count — Blood Moon affects all nonbasic lands regardless of controller, so with more than two players every opponent's nonbasic lands are hit the same way, and only lands controlled by Andre (Prismatic Omen's controller) ever get Prismatic Omen's types.

question: Ariel controls [Frostboil Snarl] and [Blood Moon]. They cast [Prismatic Omen]. After it resolves, what land types does Frostboil Snarl have?
answer:
Frostboil Snarl has all five basic land types: Plains, Island, Swamp, Mountain, and Forest — and it can tap for any color of mana.

Why: both effects apply in layer 4 (type-changing effects), in timestamp order, with no dependency between them (CR 613.1d, 613.6).

1. Blood Moon ("Nonbasic lands are Mountains") applies first. Frostboil Snarl is a nonbasic land — it lacks the "basic" supertype — even though it will have basic land types (CR 305.8, 205.4c). Setting its subtype to Mountain replaces any land types it had (it printed none) and strips the abilities generated from its rules text, so it loses "As this land enters, you may reveal an Island or Mountain card..." and "{T}: Add {U} or {R}", gaining "{T}: Add {R}" instead (CR 305.7; Blood Moon ruling #2).
2. Prismatic Omen ("Lands you control are every basic land type in addition to their other types") applies next. Because it adds types rather than setting them, Frostboil Snarl keeps Mountain and gains Plains, Island, Swamp, and Forest, along with the mana ability for each (CR 305.7, 205.1b; Prismatic Omen ruling #0).

So the final state is: Land — Plains Island Swamp Mountain Forest, with "{T}: Add {W}", "{T}: Add {U}", "{T}: Add {B}", "{T}: Add {R}", and "{T}: Add {G}". Note {R} here is red mana specifically, not generic.

Supertypes are untouched: Frostboil Snarl is still nonbasic and is not named "Mountain" (CR 205.4b, 205.4c; Blood Moon ruling #1, Prismatic Omen ruling #1). Also, Frostboil Snarl's enters-tapped/reveal ability is gone while Blood Moon is out, so it's irrelevant to a Frostboil Snarl already on the battlefield here.

Timing note: I'm assuming Blood Moon was already on the battlefield before Prismatic Omen resolved, as stated. If instead Prismatic Omen had the earlier timestamp and Blood Moon resolved later, Blood Moon would set the subtypes to just Mountain afterward, leaving only Mountain and "{T}: Add {R}". Nothing here depends on the number of players — the answer is the same in two-player and multiplayer games, since both enchantments are controlled by Ariel and Prismatic Omen only affects lands Ariel controls.

question: Adan restarts the game with [Karn Liberated]. Adan puts [Blood Moon], [Prismatic Omen] and [Winged Temple of Orazca] onto the battlefield with Karn Liberated. What colors of mana can Winged Temple of Orazca tap for?
answer:
Short answer: Winged Temple of Orazca ends up producing red only, or all five colors ({W}{U}{B}{R}{G}), depending on which of the two type-changing effects is applied last in layer 4 — and the provided rules don't include the tiebreaker (CR 613.7) for two effects that begin to exist at the same moment, since Karn Liberated puts Blood Moon, Prismatic Omen and Winged Temple of Orazca onto the battlefield simultaneously.

What each effect does:
- Blood Moon says "Nonbasic lands are Mountains." Winged Temple of Orazca is a nonbasic (Legendary) land, so its subtype is set to Mountain. Per CR 305.7 and Blood Moon ruling #2, it loses its old land types and all abilities generated from its rules text — including its printed "{T}: Add one mana of any color" and its "{1}{G}{U}, {T}" pump ability — and gains "{T}: Add {R}" (CR 305.6, Mountain).
- Prismatic Omen says lands you control are every basic land type in addition to their other types, so Winged Temple of Orazca gains Plains, Island, Swamp, Mountain and Forest and the intrinsic mana ability of each (CR 305.6, 305.7 last sentence; Prismatic Omen ruling #0): {W}{U}{B}{R}{G}.

Applying them in layer 4:
- Blood Moon first, then Prismatic Omen: subtypes become Mountain, then all five basic types → Winged Temple of Orazca taps for {W}, {U}, {B}, {R} or {G} (one mana of your choice per tap, using whichever intrinsic ability you activate).
- Prismatic Omen first, then Blood Moon: Blood Moon's "set subtype" wipes the added types → subtype is just Mountain → it taps only for {R}.

Either way, its own printed "{T}: Add one mana of any color" ability is gone, because Blood Moon's subtype-setting strips abilities generated from the land's rules text (CR 305.7).

What's missing: the rules given here don't include CR 613.7's timestamp rules or how simultaneous-entry timestamps are ordered, so I can't state from this context which of the two applies last. Note also that neither effect is dependent on the other under the dependency test — applying one doesn't change what the other does or what it applies to — so pure ordering decides it.

Assumption on timing: I'm assuming all three permanents entered the battlefield at the same time from Karn Liberated's −14. If instead one of Blood Moon or Prismatic Omen were already on the battlefield (or entered later), the later-entering one's effect would be applied second and its result above is what you'd get.

Two players vs. multiplayer: nothing here changes with player count — Blood Moon and Prismatic Omen both affect lands regardless of how many opponents are at the table (Prismatic Omen only affects lands Adan controls).

question: Apollo controls [Realmwright] naming "Island", [Arcane Adaptation] naming "Saproling", and [Life and Limb], which entered the battlefield in that order. What are the types and subtypes of Realmwright?
answer:
Realmwright ends up as a **Land Creature — Forest Island Vedalken Wizard Saproling** (no supertypes), and it's a green 1/1.

How it gets there, all in layer 4 (type-changing effects, CR 613.1d):

1. **Arcane Adaptation** (naming Saproling) makes every creature Apollo controls that type in addition to its other types, so Realmwright becomes a Vedalken Wizard Saproling (CR 205.1b — "in addition to its other types" keeps all prior types).
2. **Life and Limb** then applies, because Realmwright is now a Saproling: "All Forests and all Saprolings are 1/1 green Saproling creatures and Forest lands in addition to their other types." Realmwright gains the card type land and the land type Forest, keeping creature and its creature types. Per [Life and Limb ruling #3], the subtypes stay correlated to the right card type — Forest is a land type, Saproling/Vedalken/Wizard are creature types (CR 205.3c).
3. **Realmwright's own ability** — "Lands you control are the chosen type in addition to their other types" — now applies to Realmwright itself, because Realmwright is a land. It gains the land type Island (a basic land type, per [Realmwright ruling #1]).

Ordering note: Realmwright's ability has the earliest timestamp, but the **dependency** rule overrides timestamps here (CR 613.7, CR 613.8, CR 613.8a). Applying Life and Limb changes what Realmwright's effect applies to (it makes Realmwright a land), so Realmwright's effect is applied after Life and Limb's; likewise Life and Limb depends on Arcane Adaptation, which is also the timestamp order anyway. Importantly, because Realmwright gains Island *in addition to* its other land types, this is not a subtype-setting effect, so CR 305.7's "loses its old land types and abilities" clause does **not** kick in — Realmwright keeps Forest, keeps its own rules text, and gains the Island mana ability ({T}: Add {U}) as well as Forest's ({T}: Add {G}).

Other characteristics for completeness: Life and Limb sets the color to green in layer 5 and the power/toughness to 1/1 in layer 7b, so Realmwright is a green 1/1 (it was already 1/1). It's also now subject to summoning sickness as a land creature. Nothing here depends on the number of players — the answer is the same in a two-player or multiplayer game, since all three permanents are Apollo's own and only affect permanents Apollo controls/owns.

question: Ainsley controls [Leyline of Singularity] and [Awoken Demon] equipped with [Helm of the Host]. When the trigger from Helm of the Host resolves, will the created token be legendary?
answer:
Yes — the token ends up legendary, because Leyline of Singularity applies after the copy effect.

Helm of the Host's own text says the token is created "except the token isn't legendary," and that exception is part of the token's copiable values ([Helm of the Host ruling #3]). So as the token comes into existence it is a nonlegendary copy of Awoken Demon. But Leyline of Singularity says "All nonland permanents are legendary," a continuous effect that adds the legendary supertype to every nonland permanent Ainsley controls, including the new token. Adding a supertype doesn't remove any other supertypes ([Leyline of Singularity ruling #0], [205.4b]), and a supertype can be granted without changing card types or subtypes.

Consequence: Ainsley now controls two legendary permanents with the same name — the equipped Awoken Demon and the token copy of Awoken Demon. The legend rule is a state-based action: if a player controls two or more legendary permanents with the same name, that player chooses one and the rest go to their owners' graveyards ([704.5j], [205.4d]). So Ainsley picks one Awoken Demon to keep and the other is put into the graveyard. This is exactly the scenario described in [Leyline of Singularity ruling #2] for identically named tokens.

Assumption on timing: I'm assuming Leyline of Singularity is already on the battlefield when the Helm of the Host trigger resolves (as stated). If Leyline of Singularity were to leave the battlefield first, the token would simply be a nonlegendary Awoken Demon and the legend rule would not apply, since the rule only cares about legendary permanents.

Player count doesn't matter here: Leyline of Singularity affects all nonland permanents and the legend rule is applied per player, so the result is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table — only Ainsley's own duplicate legendaries are compared against each other.

question: Addison controls [Dryad of the Ilysian Grove] and casts [Blood Moon]. What are the characteristics of [Snow-Covered Island], [Study Hall], [Dryad Arbor], and [Mountain] after Blood Moon resolves?
answer:
Direct answer (Blood Moon has the later timestamp, so it applies after Dryad of the Ilysian Grove in layer 4; neither effect depends on the other, since 'nonbasic' is about the supertype basic, which neither effect changes):

- Snow-Covered Island — it's a basic land (supertype Basic), so Blood Moon doesn't touch it. Dryad of the Ilysian Grove gives it every basic land type: Basic Snow Land — Island Plains Swamp Mountain Forest. It has "{T}: Add {U}", "{T}: Add {W}", "{T}: Add {B}", "{T}: Add {R}", and "{T}: Add {G}" (intrinsic from each basic land type, 305.6). Colorless, no P/T. Snow is just a supertype with no function of its own [Snow-Covered Island ruling #0].
- Mountain — also basic, so likewise unaffected by Blood Moon: Basic Land — Mountain Plains Island Swamp Forest, with all five mana abilities.
- Study Hall — nonbasic, so Blood Moon overwrites it: its land subtype is set to just Mountain (it loses Plains/Island/Swamp/Forest that Dryad of the Ilysian Grove gave it). Per 305.7 it loses all abilities from its rules text, so it loses "{T}: Add {C}" and the "{1}, {T}: Add one mana of any color…" scry ability, and it has only "{T}: Add {R}" [Blood Moon ruling #2]. It's still a Land (card types don't change), still named Study Hall, still nonbasic [Blood Moon ruling #1].
- Dryad Arbor — nonbasic land, so Blood Moon applies: its land type Forest (and the extra basic types from Dryad of the Ilysian Grove) is replaced by Mountain. Setting a land's subtype doesn't touch card types or creature types (205.3c, 205.1b), so it remains a Land Creature — Mountain Dryad, still green (color indicator, [Dryad Arbor ruling #3]), still 1/1, still summoning-sick as normal. It loses the "{T}: Add {G}" it had from being a Forest and instead has "{T}: Add {R}". This matches [Dryad Arbor ruling #0] and [Dryad Arbor ruling #2]: changing its land type leaves it a green Dryad creature.

Why Blood Moon wins on the nonbasic lands: both effects are type-changing effects in layer 4, applied in timestamp order (613.6). Dryad of the Ilysian Grove adds types (305.7's "gains land types in addition" clause), then Blood Moon's "Nonbasic lands are Mountains" sets the subtype, wiping the added types. If Blood Moon had been on the battlefield first and Dryad of the Ilysian Grove entered afterward, the nonbasic lands would end up as every basic land type instead (though still without their original rules-text abilities, which Blood Moon's earlier-applied part already removed).

Multiplayer note: nothing here depends on the number of players — Blood Moon affects every nonbasic land on the battlefield regardless of controller, while Dryad of the Ilysian Grove only affects lands Addison controls.

question: Nico controls [Thespian's Stage] that's currently a copy of [Temple of Triumph]. Alayna casts [Alpine Moon] and names "Temple of Triumph" as it resolves. Alayna then activates a second Thespian's Stage targeting Temple of Triumph. What does each Thespian's Stage look like?
answer:
Direct answer: Nico's Thespian's Stage is a land named Temple of Triumph with no land types and no abilities except "{T}: Add one mana of any color" (Alpine Moon shuts it off from producing {R}/{W} and strips the copy ability). Alayna's Thespian's Stage becomes a copy of Temple of Triumph that still has the Thespian's Stage copy ability, and Alpine Moon does NOT affect it, because Alpine Moon only hits lands Alayna's opponents control.

Why:

1) Nico's Stage. Its last ability made it a copy of Temple of Triumph, "except it has this ability." The exception is part of its copiable values (707.9b), so its copiable name is Temple of Triumph and its abilities are Temple of Triumph's plus the copy ability; it lost the original "{T}: Add {C}" ability (Thespian's Stage ruling #0). Because its name is Temple of Triumph and Nico is Alayna's opponent, Alpine Moon applies: in layer 4 it loses all land types (Temple of Triumph had none printed anyway), and in layer 6 it loses all abilities — including "enters tapped," the scry trigger, "{T}: Add {R} or {W}," and the Thespian's Stage copy ability — then gains "{T}: Add one mana of any color." It keeps the land card type and any supertypes (Alpine Moon ruling #1). It also stays tapped or untapped as it already was (Thespian's Stage ruling #2). Practically, Nico can no longer activate the copy ability, since Alpine Moon removed it.

2) Alayna's Stage. Copy effects copy copiable values only; Alpine Moon's ability-removal is a continuous non-copy effect and is not copied (707.3, 707.9b). So whichever "Temple of Triumph" she targets — a real Temple of Triumph, or Nico's Stage whose copiable name is Temple of Triumph — she gets Temple of Triumph's characteristics plus "except it has this ability." If she copied Nico's Stage, the copiable values already include the Thespian's Stage ability, and her own exception grants it again; either way she has it once meaningfully. She does not enter the battlefield, so "enters tapped" and the scry trigger do nothing (Thespian's Stage ruling #1), and it doesn't untap (ruling #2). Since Alayna controls it and Alpine Moon only affects "lands your opponents control," her land keeps its abilities and taps for {R} or {W} and can re-copy later.

Self-reference note: the granted copy ability on either permanent refers to "this land" / that specific object, so activating it affects the permanent it's on, not any other object named Temple of Triumph (201.5, 201.5b, 707.11).

Multiplayer: the same analysis holds at any table size — Alpine Moon hits every opponent of Alayna's who controls a land named Temple of Triumph, and never her own lands. With more players, a third player's Stage copying Temple of Triumph would also be shut off by Alayna's Alpine Moon.

Timing note: I assumed Alpine Moon resolved (naming Temple of Triumph) before Alayna activated her Stage. If she had copied first and Alpine Moon resolved after, the result is identical, since Alpine Moon's effect applies continuously to any qualifying opponent-controlled land regardless of order.

question: Allen controls [Thraben Purebloods] which is enchanted by [Kenrith's Transformation]. Thraben Purebloods then becomes enchanted by [One with the Stars]. What happens?
answer:
Thraben Purebloods ends up as a noncreature enchantment with no abilities, green, and no creature types.

Step by step, using the layer system (rule 613.4d for power/toughness sublayers, 613.7 for timestamp order within a layer):

- Layer 4 (types): Kenrith's Transformation says the enchanted creature "is a green Elk creature" and loses its other card types/creature types. One with the Stars says the enchanted permanent "is an enchantment and loses all other card types." Both apply in layer 4, so they're ordered by timestamp (613.7); One with the Stars became attached later, so it wins. Thraben Purebloods is an enchantment only — not a creature, and not a Dog. Per One with the Stars ruling #2 it also loses subtypes tied to the card types it lost, so the Elk creature type from Kenrith's Transformation is gone too. It keeps any supertypes (it has none).
- Layer 5 (color): Kenrith's Transformation still applies — Thraben Purebloods is green (Kenrith's Transformation ruling #3).
- Layer 6 (abilities): Kenrith's Transformation's "loses all abilities" still applies. Note that One with the Stars' reminder text says "It still has its abilities," but that doesn't give abilities back; Kenrith's Transformation independently removes them, and neither effect depends on the other (613.9). Anything that grants Thraben Purebloods an ability after Kenrith's Transformation attached would stick (Kenrith's Transformation ruling #6).
- Layer 7b (base P/T): Kenrith's Transformation's base 3/3 still "applies" (613.6 — an effect keeps applying in each relevant layer even if the object is no longer the kind of thing described), but power and toughness are irrelevant while Thraben Purebloods isn't a creature.

Both Auras stay attached and legal: One with the Stars has "enchant creature or enchantment" and Thraben Purebloods is now an enchantment. Kenrith's Transformation has "enchant creature," and Thraben Purebloods is no longer a creature — so Kenrith's Transformation is attached to an illegal permanent and is put into its owner's graveyard as a state-based action. Once Kenrith's Transformation is gone, its color/ability-removal/base-P-T effects end; Thraben Purebloods reverts to being a white Dog with its own abilities, but One with the Stars keeps it an enchantment and not a creature (One with the Stars ruling #1 confirms the effect persists even when the creature-ness goes away). Note: the state-based-action rule for illegally attached Auras wasn't included in the provided context, so treat that last paragraph as the practical consequence of Kenrith's Transformation's own "enchant creature" restriction (702.5c).

This works identically in two-player and multiplayer games; nothing here depends on the number of players.

answer_gold:

question: Avery manifests the top card of their library with [Soul Summons]. Then, they mutate [Trumpeting Gnarr] targeting the manifested creature. What are the characteristics of the resulting creature if Avery chooses to put the manifested creature on top?
answer:
Direct answer: the merged permanent is a face-down 2/2 colorless creature with no name, no creature types, and no mana cost (the manifested card's face-down characteristics), but it has all of Trumpeting Gnarr's abilities in addition — including "Whenever this creature mutates, create a 3/3 green Beast creature token," which already triggered when the merge happened.

Why:
- Mutating merges the spell with the target rather than having Trumpeting Gnarr enter separately; the controller picks top or bottom, and the result is one mutated permanent represented by both cards [702.140c] [608.3d] [730.2e] [Mutating Creature Spell].
- A mutated permanent has all abilities of each card representing it, but its other characteristics (name, mana cost, color, types, power/toughness) come from the topmost component [702.140e]. With the manifested card on top, those come from the face-down manifested card, i.e. a 2/2 colorless nameless creature with no mana cost — that is what "manifest" produces (put onto the battlefield face down as a 2/2 creature, turnable face up for its mana cost if it's a creature card) per Soul Summons.
- Status is also set by the topmost component, so the merged permanent is face down [730.2e] [110.5]. These merge-derived characteristic changes are copiable and applied in layer 1a [613.2a].
- Trumpeting Gnarr's mutate trigger is an ability of a component, so the permanent has it; the mutate event occurred as the spell resolved, so Avery gets a 3/3 green Beast token.

Practical notes: any effect that referred to the mutating Trumpeting Gnarr spell now refers to the mutated permanent [702.140f]. If Avery later turns the permanent face up (paying the mana cost of the manifested card, if it's a creature card), the topmost component would then supply that card's name, cost, colors, types and power/toughness, while it still keeps Trumpeting Gnarr's abilities [702.140e]. Nothing in the provided rules covers whether a double-faced manifested card is involved; if the manifested component were double-faced, note only that a face-up merged permanent containing a double-faced component can't be turned face down [730.2j].

Assumption on timing: I'm assuming Soul Summons fully resolved before Trumpeting Gnarr was cast for its mutate cost, and that the manifested creature was still a legal target on resolution; if the target were illegal on resolution, no merge occurs and no mutate trigger happens [702.140c]. Also, the provided context contains no restriction against mutating onto a face-down creature, so this answer follows the rules as given; a face-down creature has no creature types, hence it is non-Human for Trumpeting Gnarr's targeting requirement. Player count doesn't matter here — none of the cited rules distinguish two-player from multiplayer games.

question: April casts [Spontaneous Flight] targeting their [Mist Dragon]. After that resolves April then activates its 'lose flying' ability. They cast another Spontaneous Flight targeting Mist Dragon. After that resolves they then use [Hex Parasite] to remove one flying counter. Does Mist Dragon have flying?
answer:
Yes — Mist Dragon has flying (and, assuming all of this happened in one turn, it's an 8/8 until end of turn).

Why: a flying counter grants the flying ability, so it's an ability-adding effect that works in layer 6 like any other, and the last-applied effect in that layer wins ([113.10c], [613.9], [613.7a]).

Timeline in layer 6:
1. First Spontaneous Flight resolves: Mist Dragon gets +2/+2 (layer 7c) and a flying counter — Mist Dragon has flying.
2. April activates Mist Dragon's "{0}: This creature loses flying" ability. That effect has a later timestamp, removes all instances of flying ([113.10b]), so Mist Dragon doesn't have flying — even though the counter is still physically there.
3. Second Spontaneous Flight resolves: another +2/+2 and a second flying counter. That counter's flying-granting effect has the latest timestamp, so it beats the earlier "loses flying" effect and Mist Dragon has flying again.
4. Hex Parasite removes one flying counter. One flying counter still remains on Mist Dragon, and its flying-granting effect still postdates the "loses flying" activation, so Mist Dragon still has flying.

Running the layers gives: layer 6 → loses flying (ts 2), then counter grants flying (ts 3) → Mist Dragon has flying; layer 7c → +2/+2 and +2/+2 → 8/8.

Ambiguity worth naming: the two flying counters are identical objects, so the game doesn't really distinguish "the old one" from "the new one"; either way one flying counter survives and it is a counter that was on Mist Dragon at a time after the lose-flying effect applied, so the result is the same. If instead April had activated "{0}: This creature loses flying" *after* Hex Parasite removed the counter, that later effect would win and Mist Dragon would not have flying (it could then be turned back on with "{0}: This creature gains flying").

Also note Hex Parasite gets +1/+0 until end of turn for the one counter actually removed ([Hex Parasite ruling #0]). Multiple simultaneous sources of flying would just be redundant ([702.9c]). Nothing here depends on the number of players.

question: Aimee controls [Fiend Artisan] and has four creature cards in their graveyard. Nico enchants it with [Mystic Subdual]. What is the power and toughness of Fiend Artisan?
answer:
Fiend Artisan is -1/1 (treated as 0 power for most purposes, but it is not destroyed — toughness is 1).

Why: characteristics are computed in layers (CR 613.1). Fiend Artisan's printed power/toughness is 1/1. Its "gets +1/+1 for each creature card in your graveyard" is not a characteristic-defining ability — it's a static ability generating a power/toughness-modifying effect that would apply in layer 7c (CR 613.4c).

Mystic Subdual applies in two layers (CR 613.6): "loses all abilities" in layer 6, and "-2/-0" in layer 7c. Layer 6 comes before layer 7, so by the time we reach layer 7c, Fiend Artisan has no abilities at all — the +1/+1-per-creature-card effect never starts applying, and the four creature cards in Aimee's graveyard are irrelevant. Only Mystic Subdual's -2/-0 applies: 1/1 minus 2/0 = -1/1.

Note the contrast with Mystic Subdual ruling #1: that ruling covers creatures whose power/toughness is printed as */* with a defining ability (base 0/0 once abilities are lost, so -2/0). Fiend Artisan instead has a printed 1/1, so it keeps 1/1 as its base and ends at -1/1.

Also note Fiend Artisan ruling #2: the first ability only functions on the battlefield anyway; here it's simply gone.

Timing assumption: Mystic Subdual's timestamp is later than Fiend Artisan's own ability. This doesn't matter — layer 6 always precedes layer 7c regardless of timestamps. If creature cards later enter or leave Aimee's graveyard, nothing changes while Mystic Subdual is attached; if Mystic Subdual leaves the battlefield, Fiend Artisan immediately returns to 1/1 plus +1/+1 per creature card in the graveyard.

The number of players doesn't affect this answer; the same result holds in a two-player or multiplayer game (Nico controlling the Aura doesn't change who controls Fiend Artisan).

question: Nico controls [Humility]. Avalyn controls [Maritime Guard] and wants to cast [Glowstone Recluse] mutating onto the Maritime Guard and putting it on top. What will the resulting creature's P/T be?
answer:
The mutated permanent will be a 1/1 green Spider with no abilities, and it gets no +1/+1 counters.

Why:

1. Merging is a layer 1a (copiable) effect: the mutated permanent has all abilities of each component card, and its other characteristics — including printed power/toughness — come from the topmost card, Glowstone Recluse [702.140e, 702.140c, 613.2a, 730.1]. So the starting values are a 2/3 green Spider, not Maritime Guard's 1/3.
2. Layer 6: Humility makes all creatures lose all abilities, so the merged permanent loses Reach and loses "Whenever this creature mutates, put two +1/+1 counters on it."
3. Layer 7b: Humility sets base power and toughness to 1/1 [613.4b, 208.4b]. Since Humility is the only effect setting P/T here, timestamps don't matter — the result is 1/1 [613.7].

About the mutate trigger: the merge happens as Glowstone Recluse resolves [608.3d, 702.140c], and an ability that triggers whenever a creature mutates would trigger at that moment [702.140d]. But the permanent that exists on the battlefield has already lost all abilities to Humility, so there is no mutate-trigger ability on it to trigger, and no two +1/+1 counters are ever created. (Even if counters somehow were placed, they'd apply in layer 7c and would make it 3/3 — but that isn't the case here.)

Timing note: I'm assuming Humility is already on the battlefield when Glowstone Recluse is cast and resolves, as stated. If Humility instead entered after the mutate trigger had already resolved and put counters on the permanent, those counters would survive (counters apply in layer 7c, after Humility's 7b setting) and the creature would be 3/3 with no abilities.

Player count doesn't change anything: Humility affects all creatures regardless of controller, so the answer is the same at a two-player table or a multiplayer one.

question: Alex controls [Magus of the Moon] and [Forgotten Monument]. Neil casts [Lizard, Connors's Curse] targeting Magus of the Moon. After Lizard, Connors's Curse has resolved, what are the characteristics of Forgotten Monument?
answer:
Forgotten Monument is still a nonbasic land named Forgotten Monument, but it is a Land — Mountain (no longer a Cave), colorless, with no supertypes, and its only ability is the intrinsic "{T}: Add {R}." Its own "{T}: Add {C}" and the Cave-granting ability are gone.

Why: Lizard, Connors's Curse's trigger makes Magus of the Moon lose all abilities and become a green 4/4 Lizard, and that effect doesn't end at end of turn (Lizard, Connors's Curse ruling #0). But layers run in a fixed order regardless of timestamps: type/subtype changes are applied in layer 4, while ability-removal is applied in layer 6. Magus of the Moon's "Nonbasic lands are Mountains" already applied in layer 4 to the set of nonbasic lands, and per CR 613.6 an effect that has started to apply keeps applying to that same set of objects in every applicable layer even if the ability generating it is removed. Magus of the Moon ruling #0 states this outcome explicitly: if Magus of the Moon loses its abilities, it continues to turn nonbasic lands into Mountains.

Setting a land's subtype to a basic land type (CR 305.7) makes it lose its old land types, all abilities from its rules text, and any copiable effects affecting it, and it gains "{T}: Add {R}" for Mountain (CR 305.6; Magus of the Moon ruling #4). Note {R} is red mana specifically — Forgotten Monument can no longer produce {C} (colorless mana specifically). Supertypes and the name are untouched (CR 205.4b; Magus of the Moon ruling #1), so it's still named Forgotten Monument and is still nonbasic.

Also, since Forgotten Monument's Cave-granting ability is gone and it's no longer a Cave itself, other Caves Alex controls lose that granted mana ability.

This all holds identically at a two-player or multiplayer table; Magus of the Moon affects all nonbasic lands, not just an opponent's.

question: Ainsley enchants their [Colossus Hammer] with [Rune of Flight]. Then they equip it to [Skeletal Snake]. Does Skeletal Snake have flying?
answer:
Yes — Skeletal Snake has flying, and it's a 12/11.

Why: Rune of Flight grants Colossus Hammer the ability "Equipped creature has flying." Per CR 613.7a, that granted ability's continuous effect uses Rune of Flight's timestamp, since that's later than Colossus Hammer's own timestamp. When Colossus Hammer becomes attached to Skeletal Snake it receives a new timestamp (CR 613.7e), and both of Colossus Hammer's ability effects get new timestamps too — but their relative order is preserved: "loses flying" still comes first, the Rune-granted "has flying" still comes second.

Applying that in layer 6 (ability-adding/removing): first Colossus Hammer's "Equipped creature ... loses flying" removes flying (Skeletal Snake had none anyway — see Colossus Hammer ruling #0), then the Rune-granted ability gives Skeletal Snake flying. In layer 7c, Colossus Hammer's +10/+10 makes the 2/1 Skeletal Snake a 12/11. Net result: a 12/11 Skeletal Snake with flying.

Note this is not the "gains flying later" case from Colossus Hammer ruling #2 in spirit only — the outcome matches it: an effect with a later timestamp than the loses-flying effect wins. Also, Colossus Hammer ruling #1 (an "as long as" flying ability on the creature itself) doesn't apply here, because the flying comes from an ability of Colossus Hammer itself with a later timestamp, not from a condition on Skeletal Snake.

Timing assumption: Rune of Flight was attached to Colossus Hammer *before* the equip, as stated. If instead you equipped first and then enchanted Colossus Hammer with Rune of Flight, the Rune-granted ability would still have the later timestamp, so Skeletal Snake would still have flying.

Player count doesn't matter here; nothing in this interaction depends on the number of opponents. Note that under CR 301.5d, Ainsley controls Colossus Hammer and Skeletal Snake, so there's no split-control wrinkle.

answer:
